slides.title: OO Programming Concepts

blocks.text: Object-oriented programming (OOP) involves programming using objects.
An object represents an entity in the real world. For example, a student, a desk, a circle, a button, and even a loan can all be viewed as objects.
An object has a unique identity, state, and behaviors.
The state of an object consists of a set of data fields (also known as properties) with their current values.
The behavior of an object is defined by a set of methods.

The state defines the object, and the behavior defines what the object does.

slides.title: Constructors

blocks.text: Constructors are a special kind of methods that are invoked to construct objects.
Constructors must have the same name as the class itself.
Constructors do not have a return type – not even void.
Constructors are invoked using the new operator when an object is created. They play the role of initializing objects.
A constructor with no parameters is referred to as a no-arg constructor.

to construct objects.

❑Constructors do not have a return type – not even void. 
❑Constructors are invoked using the new operator when an 
object is created. They play the role of initializing objects.
❑A constructor with no parameters is referred to as a no-arg 
constructor.

blocks.text:

slides.title: Default Constructor

blocks.text: A class may be defined without constructors.
In this case, a no-arg constructor with an empty body is implicitly defined in the class.
This constructor, called a default constructor, is provided automatically only if no constructors are explicitly defined in the class.

slides.raw_text:
Accessing Object’s Members
❑Referencing object’s data using the dot operator:
 
objectRefVar.data
 Example: myCircle.radius
❑Invoking object’s method using the dot operator:
 
objectRefVar.methodName(arguments)
 
Example: myCircle.getArea()

slides.title: Caution

blocks.text: Recall that you use: Math.methodName(arguments); to invoke a method in the Math class.
Example: Math.pow(3, 2.5);
Can you invoke getArea() using Circle.getArea()?
The answer is no. All the methods used in Math are static, which are defined using the static keyword.
However, getArea() is non-static. It must be invoked from

an object using: objectRefVar.getArea(arguments);
Example: myCircle.getArea();

slides.title: Differences between Variables of Primitive Data Types and Object Types

blocks.text: Every variable represents a memory location that holds a value.
When you declare a variable, you are telling the compiler what type of value the variable can hold.
A variable of a primitive type holds a value of the primitive type, and a variable of a reference type holds a reference to where an object is stored in memory.

slides.title: Garbage Collection and the null value

blocks.text: As shown in the previous figure, after the assignment c1 = c2, c1 points to the same object referenced by c2.
The object previously referenced by c1 is no longer referenced. This object is known as garbage. Garbage is automatically collected by the Java Virtual Machine.

If you know that an object is no longer needed, you can explicitly assign null to a reference variable for the object. The JVM will automatically collect the space if the object is not referenced by any variable.
The null value means referencing nothing in memory.

blocks.text: The default value of a data field is null for a reference type
The default value is 0 for a numeric type
The default value is false for a boolean type
The default value is '\u0000' for a char type.
Java assigns no default value to a local variable inside a method.

slides.title: Instance versus Static Variables,

blocks.text: Constants, and Methods
Instance variables belong to a specific object of a class.
Instance methods are invoked by an object of a class.
Static variables are shared by all the instances of the class.
They are known as class variables.
Static methods are not tied to a specific object.
Static methods cannot access instance data fields and instance methods of the class.
Static constants are final variables shared by all the instances of the class.

slides.raw_text:
Instance versus Static Variables,
Constants, and Methods
❑Instance variables belong to a specific object of a class.
❑Instance methods are invoked by an object of a class.
❑Static variables are shared by all the instances of the class. 
They are known as class variables.
❑Static methods are not tied to a specific object.
❑Static methods cannot access instance data fields and 
instance methods of the class.
❑Static constants are final variables shared by all the 
instances of the class.

slides.title: Instance versus Static Methods

blocks.text: An instance method can invoke an instance or static method. It can also access an instance or static data field.
A static method can only invoke a static method and access a static data field.
A static method cannot invoke an instance method or access an instance data field, since static methods and static data fields don’t belong to a particular object.

slides.title: Visibility Modifiers and Accessor/Mutator Methods

blocks.text: By default, the class, variable, or method can be accessed by any class in the same package.
public
The class, data, or method is visible to any class in any package.
private
The data or methods can be accessed only by the declaring class.
The get and set methods are used to read and modify private data.

slides.raw_text:
Visibility Modifiers and 
Accessor/Mutator Methods
❑By default, the class, variable, or method can be accessed by any 
class in the same package. 
❑public
The class, data, or method is visible to any class in any package. 
❑private 
The data or methods can be accessed only by the declaring class.
❑The get and set methods are used to read and modify private data.

slides.title: Example of Visibility Modifiers

blocks.text: The private modifier restricts access to within a class.
The public modifier enables unrestricted access.
The default modifier (no modifier is used) restricts access to within a package.

slides.raw_text:
Example of Visibility Modifiers
❑The private modifier restricts access to within a class.
❑The public modifier enables unrestricted access. 
❑The default modifier (no modifier is used) restricts access to 
within a package.

slides.title: Immutable Objects and Classes

blocks.text: If the contents of an object cannot be changed once the object is created, the object is called immutable, and its class is called an immutable class.
If you delete the set method in the Circle class, the class would be immutable because radius is private and cannot be changed without a set method.
A class with all private data fields and without mutators is not necessarily immutable. The following class Student has all private data fields and no mutators, but it is mutable.

blocks.text: The scope of instance and static variables is the entire class.
They can be declared anywhere inside a class.
The scope of a local variable starts from its declaration and continues to the end of the block that contains the variable.
A local variable must be initialized before it is used.
The compiler will generate an error message if you use a local variable without initialization.

slides.raw_text:
Scope of Variables
❑The scope of instance and static variables is the entire class. 
They can be declared anywhere inside a class.
❑The scope of a local variable starts from its declaration and 
continues to the end of the block that contains the variable.
❑A local variable must be initialized before it is used.
❑The compiler will generate an error message if you use a 
local variable without initialization.

slides.title: The Keyword this

blocks.text: The keyword this is the name of a reference that refers to an object itself.
One common use of the keyword this is reference a class’s hidden data fields.
Another common use of the keyword this is to enable a constructor to invoke another constructor of the same class.
